title: Pauri 29, sound: bhugat giaan

cards: Mealtime in a yogi camp. The one who keeps the stores walks down the line, handing out the shared food, and somebody blows a small horn; the note hangs in the evening air.
Commentators say the yogis had their own word for that meal: bhugat. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak meeting and talking with yogis on his travels.
Yesterday he took their earrings and their ash and turned them inward. Today he sits down at their dinner, and the first line of Pauri 29 is built from what's on the table.

teach.h: BHUGAT GIAAN — WISDOM IS THE MEAL.
teach.b: Here is the first line of Pauri 29, as Guru Nanak sang it: bhugat giaan daiaa bhanddaaran, ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. One word at a time. Bhugat: the meal handed out in the yogis' gathering.
Giaan: wisdom, knowing. So bhugat giaan: let wisdom be the meal.
Daiaa: compassion. Bhanddaaran: the one who keeps the storeroom and serves from it. The word even has a feminine ending, the woman of the stores.
So compassion is the one holding the ladle. Then the second half changes its sound.
Ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. A ghatt is a clay pot, and in the Granth it often means the body, or the heart inside it. Ghatt ghatt: in every pot, in every heart.
Vaajeh: they play, they ring. Naad: the note, the sound, the same word the yogis used for the call of their horn. In every heart, the note is sounding.

teach.h: A LINE BUILT LIKE A MEAL.
teach.b: Now hear how the line is built.

The first half is four solid words, set down like dishes on a cloth: bhugat, giaan, daiaa, bhanddaaran. The second half doubles a word, ghatt ghatt, then rings out on naad, the way a horn might close a meal.
And like the stanzas around it, this one ends with a refrain taken from the yogis' own greeting: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him, my salute. The whole meaning comes tomorrow.
Today, just the sound, and the two words that start it: bhugat giaan.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning as part of Nitnem; pauris 28 to 31 are often heard as Guru Nanak answering the Nath yogis in their own vocabulary, and each ends with the refrain aades tisai aades.

s: Pauri 29 borrows words from the yogis' own camp life
bhugat, the shared meal, and naad, the call of the horn, were yogi words.
in the Granth, ghatt only ever means a clay pot
it often stands for the body, or the heart inside it.
the refrain aades tisai aades echoes the yogis' own greeting
Nanak turns their greeting into a salute to the One.

games.q: you're a hungry yogi in the meal line. in Pauri 29, what does Guru Nanak say should fill your bowl?
games.why: bhugat giaan: let wisdom be the meal, and compassion the one who serves it.

practice: Say the first line aloud three times, slowly: bhugat giaan daiaa bhanddaaran, ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad, the first half steady in four even steps, the second half ringing.
Then stop, and listen for whatever is still sounding in you after the words end. When a thought wanders in, come back by whispering ghatt ghatt, in every heart.

wordCard.voice: Naad, the note, the sound. The stanza where Guru Nanak sits down at the yogis' meal: wisdom is the food, compassion serves it, and a note sounds in every heart.
